newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-TSHWETE KEEPS ENQUIRY THREAT IN RESERVE.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-TSHWETE KEEPS ENQUIRY THREAT IN RESERVE.

text.p: South African Sports Minister Steve Tshwete has been granted the power to set up a commission of inquiry into the running of rugby -- but he will not impose it yet.
Tshwete was given the permission by President Nelson Mandela on Tuesday, but after meeting rugby task force chairman Mthobi Tyamzashe, the minster to postpone its implementation.
In a statement issued on Wednesday, Tshwete said he "remained upbeat" about the imminence of an inquiry.
But Tyamzashe, who is also director-general of Tswhete's ministry of sport and recreation, asked for time to conclude their own findings before deciding on a commission.

Tshwete set up the task force in February to investigate allegations of corruption in the running of rugby as well as general concerns over the pace of development and the extent of racism in the sport.
The South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) reluctantly agreed to cooperate with the task force, but last week ordered their provinces not to talk to the team.

SARFU backed down on Monday but issued an ultimatum: unless they were furnished with full details of the allegations against them by August 15 they would seek a court order compelling the minister to release them.

In a barely disguised reference to SARFU president Louis Luyt, Tshwete added in his statement that he was determined to show SARFU that he would not tolerate sports adminsitrators who were insensitive to public opinion or who assumed ownership of the sports in which they had been elected to serve.
A spokesman for SARFU said they would make no comment until it was finally known whether they were to face a commission of inquiry.
